sources.note: No prosodic statement about Cahuarano/Aámuuwáaja. The entry says 'Cahuarano, an ethnic group speaking a language mutually intelligible with Iquito but considered distinct, at least in part due to the fact that Iquitos considered the Aámuuwáaja a nomadic people.. The last capture of Aámuuwáaja individuals occurred in the 1920s or 1930s, and they have not been seen since'; sec. 1.2.9: 'A fifth group, the Aámuuwaaja, which modern Iquito elders describe as a hunter-gatherer group, is considered to be closely related, but socially distinct from the Iquito groups'; sec. 1.2.8 says Iquito ideologies…

sources.note: No rule. 'Cahuarano or Moracano - spoken on the Pucacuro River in the same region. [Tessmann 1930, pp. 526-527.]' Its 11-item Cahuarano list (from Tessmann) carries acute accents on assorted syllables (pá-nak, poí-nami, inámi, nianamí, itémo, shekárok, musiténa, kómu) -- transcription marks only, no statement.

sources.citation: Mason, J. Alden. 1950. 'The languages of South American Indians'. In Julian H. Steward (ed.), Handbook of South American Indians, vol. 6 (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 143), 157-317. Washington: Smithsonian Institution.
sources.note: 'Tessmann (1930) considers the Iguito independent, divided into two groups, the Iguito or Iguito Proper and the Cahuarano or Kawarano; he calls it a mixed Tukano-Pano language. Steward and Metraux.. believe that this is erroneous, that the Iguito language is very similar to Gae, and that Tessmann's Cahuarano may be Maracano.' Classification only, no phonology.

sources.citation: Steward, Julian H. & Alfred Métraux. 1948. 'Tribes of the Peruvian and Ecuadorian Montaña'. In J. H. Steward (ed.), Handbook of South American Indians, vol. 3: The Tropical Forest Tribes (BAE Bulletin 143), 535-656. Washington: Smithsonian Institution.
sources.note: 'Tessmann erroneously classed modern Iquito as a distinct language, and named two divisions, the Iquito and the Cahuarano (Tessmann, 1930), the latter perhaps being the older Maracano.' Ethnographic, no phonology.
